extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for judging empirical generalizations, detecting causation versus chance, and calculating probability; covers limits of empirical laws, signs of derivative laws, elimination of chance by averaging, and Laplace's formulation of probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical laws valid only within observed limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws can only be received as true within the limits of time and place (and circumstance) in which they have been found true by observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because empirical laws depend on unknown collocations or on laws not yet resolved, they cannot be confidently extended beyond observed time/place/circumstance. Treat results of simple observation (without experiment) as empirical laws until further confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement alone does not establish causation
rubrics_metrics.description: When the only proof for a generalization is the Method of Agreement, the generalization is only an empirical law and does not prove causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Method of Agreement can only ascertain common circumstances across cases but cannot distinguish the true cause from collateral or derivative uniformities; such conclusions require confirmation by the Method of Difference or deductive explanation (accounting à priori).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to confirm empirical generalizations by Method of Difference or deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: An observed uniformity must be either confirmed by the Method of Difference or explained deductively (accounted for à priori) before it can be treated as a law of causation rather than an empirical law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until so explained, uniformities remain empirical and lack the highest degree of certainty. Use experiment (difference) or connect to ultimate laws to elevate status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign of derivative law: evidence of intermediate link(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is evidence (or reasonable surmise) of intermediate phenomenon(s) between antecedent A and consequent B, then the law 'A causes B' is likely derivative, resolvable into laws involving those intermediates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for phenomena (denoted x) that plausibly intervene (e.g., corpuscular processes in chemistry or physiology). Presence of such intermediates implies the observed law is compound and not ultimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign of derivative law: extremely complex antecedent
rubrics_metrics.description: When the antecedent is extremely complex (composed of many homogeneous or heterogeneous parts), the observed sequence is probably compound and resolvable into simpler laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because effects of a composite antecedent are ordinarily the sum of effects of its parts (Composition of Causes), complex antecedents (e.g., meteorological states, organized nature) suggest derivative, not ultimate, laws. Use decomposition or account for component causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical-law authority varies with presumptive resolvability
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws have varying degrees of authority depending on whether there is reason to presume they are resolvable into simpler laws alone or into laws plus particular collocations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequences tied to progressive stages of a common cause (e.g., organism life stages) have stronger empirical status than those likely depending on particular collocations (e.g., local stratigraphic order). Assess plausibility of resolution into simpler laws when judging strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: 'chance' as lack of grounds for inferring uniformity (coincidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: An event 'by chance' is better characterized as a coincidence from which we have no ground to infer an uniformity: phenomena conjoined without reason to expect their recurrence (i.e., not related through causation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assert production by 'chance' in the sense of lawlessness; rather treat casual conjunctions as effects of unrelated causes. Distinguish single accidental conjunctions from repeatable law-based conjunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base-rate consideration: account for marginal frequencies when assessing coincidence
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge whether a coincidence between A and B indicates a law, deduct from the observed frequency the amount expected purely from the absolute frequencies (base rates) of A and B occurring independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if A occurs in 1/2 of cases and B in 1/3, expected co-occurrence without connexion is 1/6. Only the excess above that expected value counts as evidence for a causal connexion. Always compute expected coincidence from marginal rates before inferring law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of trivial coincidences when one phenomenon is ubiquitous
rubrics_metrics.description: If one phenomenon (A) exists always or very frequently, its co-occurrence with others does not imply causation; maximal frequency of coincidence can still be casual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: fixed stars coexist with all observed phenomena but are not their cause. High absolute co-occurrence is not evidence unless it exceeds what the ubiquity of A makes inevitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative-frequency test for connexion between non-ubiquitous phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: If A occurs in a larger proportion of cases where B is present than where B is absent (and vice versa), then there is some connexion through causation between A and B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare conditional proportions P(A|B) vs P(A|not B) (or P(B|A) vs P(B|not A)). A greater proportion than expected indicates either common causes or causal influence; a smaller proportion indicates repugnance or counteracting causes. Use comparative frequencies rather than raw co-occurrence counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: judge coincidence by whether frequency exceeds chance expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: The question is whether the observed frequency of coincidence is more than chance will account for — i.e., more than might rationally be expected if the coincidence were casual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No universal numerical threshold is given; the determination is case-specific and depends on the frequencies of the component phenomena and the context. Use expected rates and assess excess or deficit accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of Causes and mixed law/chance effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When a constant cause A produces an effect that is successively modified by many variable (changeable) causes, the observed result blends law (effect of A) and chance (effects of variable causes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If variable causes cannot be excluded, hold A fixed and make many trials across varying conditions; the mean of results approximates the effect of A alone, while deviations around the mean are due to chance (variable causes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of chance by averaging (law extraction by mean)
rubrics_metrics.description: To eliminate the effects of numerous indeterminate modifying causes, repeat experiments preserving A and take as many trials as possible; if results oscillate about a stable mean, that mean is the effect due to A and the remainder is chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sufficiency is tested when further increases in trials do not materially change the average. Examples: repeated measurements to cancel experimental errors, discovering diurnal barometer variation, detecting loaded dice. Use sample size until average stabilizes within required accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of residual (small) constant causes via mean of many trials
rubrics_metrics.description: If an effect is chiefly due to changeable causes but possibly has a small constant component, take a large number of trials; if the average does not converge to zero but to a small nonzero value, that residual is attributable to a constant cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the method for detecting subtle biases (e.g., loaded dice) or small systematic effects hidden by larger variable fluctuations. Increase trials until the mean stabilizes to reveal the residual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample-size sufficiency is case-dependent (no universal rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no general answer to how many instances are required to deem a coincidence non-casual; the number depends on context and the principle that larger samples reduce the effect of chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide sufficiency by the stability of averages or proportions in the context at hand, and by comparing observed deviation to what chance plausibly produces. For formal quantification, resort to the doctrine of chances/theory of probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplacean calculation of probabilities via equally possible cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability can be measured by reducing events to a number of equally possible cases (equally undecided as to their existence) and taking the ratio of favorable cases to all possible cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two prerequisites: (1) among the events some one will certainly happen and no more than one, and (2) we have no reason to favor any particular event. In practice, equality of cases is often justified by prior experience (frequencies) or deductive symmetry (e.g., mechanical symmetry of a fair coin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equally probable assignment may require empirical or deductive grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: To treat two outcomes as equally probable, it is not sufficient to be indifferent; we often rely on experience showing equal frequency, or deductive grounds (symmetry) that enforce equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: coin toss is deemed 50/50 because repeated trials show near-equal frequency, or because of mechanical symmetry and forces. Use empirical frequency evidence or theoretical symmetry to justify equiprobability assumptions.
